text: You get a binary search tree and two nodes in it, p and q. Return their lowest common ancestor — the deepest node that has both of them under it.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — this is a BST, not a plain binary tree. So every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than it, and every value on the right is bigger. Is that right?
Correct. All values are unique too.

Good. Then here is the thing I want to say up front: I don't have to search for anything. In a general binary tree I'd have to find p and q first. In a BST the values tell me which way to go, so this is not a search, it is a descent. Let me put it as an interval: lo is the smaller of the two values, hi the bigger. At any node there are only three answers. Bigger than hi — both targets are on the left, so I go left. Smaller than lo — I go right. Otherwise the node is inside the range, the two targets split here, and that node is the answer.
One more question, and it matters more than it sounds. Can a node be its own ancestor?
Yes. The problem says so directly — a node is allowed to be a descendant of itself.

That is what I hoped. It fits the interval picture with no extra work. If p itself is the split node, then p equals lo, and lo is still inside the closed range. So the same inside-means-stop rule already returns it. I don't need a special case — but I do need my comparisons to be strict, and I'll come back to that in the code. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Between two and ten to the fifth nodes. Values are unique and fit in an int, roughly plus or minus ten to the ninth. Both p and q are guaranteed to exist in the tree.

I want to say that last one out loud as an assumption I am leaning on. My solution will have no null check, and it is safe only because of that promise. Let me run through the example. The tree is six, two, eight, zero, four, seven, nine, null, null, three, five, with p two and q four. Node four sits in the right subtree of node two, and a node is its own ancestor, so the answer is node two. That matches the expected output.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to ignore that this is a BST: walk the whole tree, record the path from the root to p and to q, and take the last node they share. That works, but it is linear time and linear space, and it throws away the one thing that makes this problem interesting. This problem reminds me of binary search. In binary search I compare the target to the middle and drop half the array. Here I compare the range to the current node and drop a whole subtree. Same two-way decision, just walking pointers instead of indices.

Here's the plan. One: compute lo and hi from the two values. Two: if hi is smaller than the node, go left; if lo is bigger, go right. Three: otherwise the node is inside the range — return it. The invariant: the answer is always inside the subtree I'm standing on, because I only ever drop a side that holds neither target. One thing worth flagging — the first node inside the range is the answer, and I can stop. Below it, one target goes left and the other goes right, so no deeper node has both. There's a trade-off here. Recursion reads cleanly, but every call is a tail call, so it can also be a constant-space loop. I'll write the recursion first and mention the loop at the end. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. Three branches, one comparison each, no bookkeeping. One thing worth flagging — the two comparisons are less-than and greater-than, and they have to be strict. That is a correctness requirement, and it is exactly the own-ancestor case. If I loosen the first one to less-or-equal and p itself is the split node, so the max equals the node, the strict version stops and returns it. The loose version says still go left, and walks past the answer into a subtree it can never come back up from.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Same tree, p two and q four, so lo is two and hi is four, and I expect node two. The row that matters is the second call, at node two. Four is not less than two, and two is not greater than two — that is where strictness earns its keep. With greater-or-equal I'd have gone right, past the answer. Both tests fail, so it returns node two. Two calls. Let's also test with corner cases. Two and eight split at the root: node six, one call. Three and five, the deepest split: node four, three calls. Zero and five, both under two: node two, two calls. The call count is always the depth of the answer plus one.
You keep saying the strict comparison is load-bearing. How sure are you?

Sure enough that I checked it by brute force. Every BST on the values zero to n minus one, for n up to eight — two thousand fifty-five trees — and every ordered pair p, q: a hundred eighteen thousand six hundred twenty-one triples. Strict comparisons: zero failures. Less-or-equal: fifty-four thousand two hundred eighty-three failures, and they are exactly the triples where the answer is the larger target — the own-ancestor case, nothing else. The surprise is that most of those failures do not crash. About seventy-one percent quietly return a wrong node, because the subtree it walks into still holds the other target. In the example tree, zero and two should give two; the loose version returns zero. Always wrong on that set, and usually silent about it — the worse failure mode.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is O of h, the height — exactly the depth of the answer plus one; on a balanced tree, O of log n. The space complexity is O of h for the call stack. In the worst-case scenario the tree is a sorted chain, ten to the fifth deep. At O two the compiler turns the tail call into a loop. At O zero it doesn't, and an eight-megabyte stack survives with a margin of only about one point three. I'd rather not depend on the compiler, so here is the loop: same three branches, constant space, and it agrees with the recursion on every triple. Oh, one more thing — no null check is deliberate, safe only because both targets exist. Break that promise and it usually returns a wrong node rather than crashing.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You reframed it before writing anything — a descent instead of a search, and the two nodes as one interval, so the three-way test fell out on its own. You treated the strict comparisons as a correctness requirement, measured it, and named the silent-wrong-answer split most people miss. And you didn't stop at quoting O of h space: you noticed the tail call, checked what the compiler really does, and still offered the loop so the guarantee doesn't rest on the compiler. Good work.
